mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes heat from work?

options.A: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, whereas work is energy transferred when a force acts through a distance.
options.B: Heat is energy transferred when a force acts through a distance, whereas work is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
options.C: Both heat and work are forms of energy stored within a system.
options.D: Heat and work are identical and can be used interchangeably.

mcqs.answer: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, whereas work is energy transferred when a force acts through a distance.
mcqs.explanation: Heat is the transfer of energy that occurs solely due to a temperature gradient between system and surroundings. Work, on the other hand, is the transfer of energy that results when a macroscopic force acts through a distance (e.g., volume change against pressure). Options B, C, and D misrepresent these definitions.

mcqs.question: A gas expands reversibly against a constant external pressure. According to the sign convention used in physics, what is the sign of the work done on the system?

options.D: It depends on the temperature change

mcqs.explanation: In the common sign convention for thermodynamics, work done by the system on the surroundings is taken as positive, while work done on the system is taken as negative. During expansion the system does work on the surroundings, so the work on the system is negative. Options A, C, and D are therefore incorrect.

mcqs.learning_point: Calculate work in simple thermodynamic processes
mcqs.question: Consider two processes for 1 mol of ideal gas at 300 K: (i) isobaric expansion from 10 L to 20 L at 1 atm, (ii) isochoric heating from 300 K to 600 K at 10 L. Which process results in a larger magnitude of work done by the gas?
mcqs.explanation: Work in an isobaric (constant‑pressure) expansion is W = PΔV, which is non‑zero (1 atm × 10 L). In an isochoric (constant‑volume) process, ΔV = 0, so W = 0. Hence the isobaric expansion yields a larger magnitude of work. Options B, C, and D are therefore incorrect.

mcqs.question: In a pressure‑volume (P‑V) diagram for a cyclic process, the net work done by the system during one complete cycle is equal to:

options.A: The area under the curve for the expansion part only
options.B: The area enclosed by the cycle
options.C: The slope of the curve at any point
options.D: The product of the maximum pressure and maximum volume

mcqs.answer: The area enclosed by the cycle
mcqs.explanation: For a closed loop on a P‑V diagram, the net work done by the system equals the algebraic area enclosed by the loop (work done during expansion minus work during compression). Option A ignores the compression part, while C and D are unrelated to the definition of work on a P‑V diagram.

mcqs.question: Heat and work are both modes of energy transfer. Which of the following correctly describes them?

options.A: Heat transfer occurs due to temperature difference; work transfer occurs due to macroscopic force acting through a distance.
options.B: Heat transfer occurs due to force acting through a distance; work transfer occurs due to temperature difference.
options.C: Both heat and work require a temperature gradient.
options.D: Neither heat nor work involves transfer of energy.

mcqs.answer: Heat transfer occurs due to temperature difference; work transfer occurs due to macroscopic force acting through a distance.
mcqs.explanation: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature gradient, while work is energy transferred when a force moves something through a distance (e.g., volume change against pressure). Options B, C, and D misstate these definitions.

mcqs.question: According to the sign convention commonly adopted in thermodynamics, the work term W is taken as:

options.A: Positive when work is done on the system
options.B: Negative when work is done on the system

mcqs.answer: Negative when work is done on the system
mcqs.explanation: The standard sign convention assigns a negative sign to work done on the system (i.e., when the surroundings do work on the system) and a positive sign to work done by the system. Options A, C, and D do not follow this convention.

mcqs.learning_point: Calculate work in simple thermodynamic processes
mcqs.question: The work done by an ideal gas during a constant‑pressure (isobaric) expansion from volume V₁ to V₂ is given by:
mcqs.explanation: For an isobaric process, pressure remains constant, so work equals pressure multiplied by the change in volume: W = PΔV. The other expressions either invert the relationship or introduce incorrect terms.

mcqs.question: A gas changes from state (P₁, V₁) to (P₂, V₂) along a straight line on a P‑V diagram. How is the work done by the gas during this process calculated?

options.A: By multiplying the average pressure ((P₁+P₂)/2) by the change in volume (V₂ – V₁)
options.B: By multiplying the initial pressure P₁ by the change in volume
options.C: By multiplying the final pressure P₂ by the change in volume
options.D: By taking the product of the pressure difference and volume difference

mcqs.answer: By multiplying the average pressure ((P₁+P₂)/2) by the change in volume (V₂ – V₁)
mcqs.explanation: When the path on a P‑V diagram is a straight line, the pressure varies linearly. The work equals the area under the line, which is the average pressure times ΔV. Options B and C use only one pressure value, and D uses an incorrect product of differences.
